page: Amazon Web Services c6in.2xlarge is a compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon 8375C processor running at a clock speed of 3.5 GHz. The instance provides 8 dedicated vCPUs across 4 physical cores with hyper-threading. It is equipped with 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory operating at 3 GHz, which translates to 2.0 GB of RAM per core. The processor includes a 54 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512, AVX512_VNNI, and cryptographic acceleration via AES and SHA_NI. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators.

In terms of performance, the c6in.2xlarge demonstrates average capabilities across most standard benchmarks. It achieves a stress-ng single-core score of 1889.79 and a multi-core score of 7714.83. Memory bandwidth is measured at 412.8 GB/sec for small cached blocks and 48.61 GB/sec for large uncached blocks. However, performance bottlenecks are evident in decompression and machine learning workloads. The instance registers weak performance in single-threaded and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, scoring 8.21 GB/sec and 25.44 GB/sec respectively. Additionally, LLM inference speeds for a medium 7B model are poor, yielding only 15.51 tokens per second for prompt processing and 7.63 tokens per second for text generation.

The c6in.2xlarge is qualitatively cost-efficient for network-intensive and compute-bound workloads that do not require local NVMe storage or massive memory footprints. With a baseline network bandwidth of 12 Gbps, it is well-suited for static web serving, which achieves a throughput of 12.28 GB/sec, and high-throughput key-value store operations, as shown by a Redis SET performance of 7.93 million operations per second. Other appropriate workloads include software compilation, image processing, and general-purpose dedicated compute tasks.

Operating at 3.5 GHz, it features 8 dedicated vCPUs, 4 physical cores, and 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory. The instance lacks local storage and GPUs, relying instead on network-attached storage and offering a baseline network bandwidth of 12 Gbps. Benchmark data indicates average performance across most compute and memory tests, with a Geekbench multi-core score of 5599.0 and a Redis SET throughput of 7.93 million operations per second. This instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for dedicated compute tasks, making it suitable for static web serving, software compilation, and key-value database operations.
